extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and research mathematicians (especially algebraic geometers) interested in rigor, proof practice, and objectivity
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly analysis comparing conceptions of mathematical rigor and objectivity (small-scale/formal vs large-scale/substantial) with a historical case study of the Italian School of algebraic geometry; evaluates effects on reliability, shareability, and mathematical practice. Useful for assessing what makes proofs or arguments acceptable, communicable, and objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor as formalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is rigorous if it can be converted into a formal proof; with any given proof it should be possible, given enough resources, to produce a formal proof down to axioms and rules of a formal foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted characterization from the received view and Avigad: 'formalization is continuous with the usual mathematical procedures for making claims and arguments precise.' Applicable across areas of mathematics; formalizability is treated as the canonical test for rigor. No explicit scoring, but functions as the standard against which non-formal practices are judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-scale rigor (Enriques' small-scale logic / formal rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerned with refined analysis of exact thought processes: decomposition of inferences into smaller inferences enabling local, step-by-step grasping and mechanical/verifiable checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes detailed, mechanically checkable proofs (formal proofs or highly detailed informal proofs). Examples: proof assistants (Coq, Lean) that require a 'pixel-by-pixel' description. Advantages: enables intersubjectivity/shareability and mechanical verification. Anti-patterns/downsides: excessive fussy detail can obscure overall strategy and hinder holistic understanding; may make the 'map of the woods' hard to see.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large-scale rigor (Enriques' large-scale logic / Severi's substantial rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pertains to the organic, macroscopic structure of arguments and theories; a holistic grasp of how arguments and major lemmas relate across areas—often tied to intuition and visual 'seeing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severi calls this 'substantial rigor' (faithfulness to the geometrical datum) as opposed to axiomatic formal rigor. Advantages: can better lead to faithful descriptions of mathematical facts and enable 'enlightenment' or insight. Downsides: may be non-shareable, elitist, allow unnoticed gaps and errors, and hinder local verification if details cannot be supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial rigor (Severi's formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor conceived as essential faithfulness to the geometrical datum rather than strict axiomatic completeness; legitimate when used as an expression of an intuitive fact to be proved later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severi: acceptable when the principle can be later formalized or given axiomatic footing; legitimate use when it 'becomes an axiom with an effective field applicability.' Risk: when substantial rigor is used without later formal justification it can produce gappy or incorrect literature (example: late-period Severi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of simil-proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Simil-proofs: arguments that look like proofs and are accepted by relevant agents but may contain fatal errors; reliability is the likelihood that a simil-proof is a genuine correct proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor underwrites the reliability of simil-proofs—different simil-proofs embody different types of rigor and therefore different reliability. Even rigorous appearant proofs can be fallacious; assessing reliability involves how well the argument supports its conclusion and the possibility of grasping that support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability (arguments must be shareable to count as evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument is shareable if its content and supposed correctness could be grasped by relevantly trained human minds from a (possibly enthymematic) perceptible presentation of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shareability is necessary for objectivity-as-intersubjectivity; methods relying on private visual 'seeing' (e.g., Enriques's visions) fail this test and lead to communication impasses. Shareability demands that presentations enable others to grasp correctness; lack of shareability undermines the community's ability to check and build upon results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grasping: local (step-by-step) vs holistic (large-scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two modes of understanding how an argument supports its conclusion: (1) local: step-by-step grasping with acceptance of premises; (2) holistic: awareness of overall structure and relation to broader mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-scale rigor underwrites local grasping; large-scale rigor underwrites holistic grasping. Both are valuable and distinct: local grasping allows mechanical verification and intersubjectivity; holistic grasping provides insight and may more directly track facts. Evaluation should consider which grasp(s) a presentation enables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between detailed formalization and overall strategy in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good mathematical presentation should give enough local detail to allow checking while also providing hints to overall strategy to enable holistic grasping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: a sequence of deductive steps without hints to overall strategy (can hide irreparable errors); an overburdened proof with fussy details may obstruct the overall view. Recommended practice: include maps of overall strategy and discovery clues alongside the steps; Burgess' observation: experts may find outlines more compelling than buried details if the latter obscure strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity as faithfulness to the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity conceived as correctness or faithful description of mathematical facts: 'if a claim is objective, it correctly describes some aspect of the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linked to large-scale/substantial rigor and the Italian School's quasi-concrete approach. Strength: can lead to substantial advances. Weakness: may be elitist (dependent on exceptional visual insight) and non-shareable, risking unverified or incorrect results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity as intersubjectivity (absence of personal bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity conceived as freedom from personal biases achieved through social processes and shareable evidence—results must be independent of individual preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized via shareability and small-scale rigor: mathematical arguments become 'agreed-upon evidence' only when they can be grasped and checked by trained others. This conception is democratizing and necessary for sustained community practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal mechanization and proof assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanized formal proofs (via proof assistants) produce fully detailed, mechanically checkable formal proofs readable by machines and humans unable to 'see' intuitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: proof assistants are like printers specifying pixels; they enforce small-scale rigor and enable absolute mechanical verification. Trade-off: they can obscure or fail to present the overall strategy and holistic meaning; formalization is continuous with ordinary practice but may require effort and can change presentation style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intuition and visualization (permissible when connectable to formal detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual intuition and 'seeing' can be legitimate parts of mathematical practice when their spatial/visual content can be spelled out in mathematical terms and ultimately connected to formalizable arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue visual reasoning can be rigorous if convertible into detailed arguments; purely private visual insight that cannot be communicated or formalized undermines shareability and intersubjective objectivity. Historical note: Italian School exploited intuition heavily, sometimes without later formal justification, producing both breakthroughs and problematic gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability and longevity of mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical method or practice must be communicable and usable by different mathematicians to flourish; practices only accessible to exceptionally talented individuals cannot sustain a community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical implication: the Italian School's reliance on non-shareable seeing limited its long-term viability. Evaluation criteria for methods should include whether they can be taught, shared, and applied by a broader community.
